rationale: A broad scouting gradient should reveal the full elution window while limiting the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The midpoint temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shortening the gradient tests whether we can retain full resolution while reducing elution time, with the minimum resolution of 2.68 providing a useful margin.

The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair close to the resolution threshold. Raising temperature at fixed gradient tests whether selectivity improves while shortening retention further.
At 50 C the critical pair improved to R = 2.10 while maximum CRF was preserved. Shortening the gradient by one grid step tests whether that selectivity gain permits a faster fully resolved method.

Narrowing the solvent window makes the six-minute gradient slightly shallower than the fully resolved eight-minute method. Raising the starting organic fraction should reduce retention while keeping it below the estimated first-peak elution composition.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving the slope of injection 5 to reduce elution time. This tests how far the starting organic fraction can increase before early-peak compression or a selectivity change sacrifices full resolution.

The last peak in injection 6 exited near 0.50 organic, so an endpoint of 0.60 should suffice. This trimmed four-minute gradient is slightly shallower, aiming to strengthen the marginal critical pair while reducing programmed gradient duration.

Raise the solvent window one step while preserving injection 7's slope to seek faster elution. This tests whether its resolution margin can tolerate further compression of the early and critical pairs.

Reduce the endpoint one step to make injection 8's gradient shallower and recover the critical pair's resolution. Keeping the higher starting organic fraction may preserve a retention-time advantage over injection 7.

Maximum CRF is already secured, so test a much faster gradient for a second fully resolved region beyond the critical pair's possible elution-order crossover. Returning to 40 C should help separate the early pair under this steeper gradient.

Test the low-temperature limit at the same fast gradient to assess whether temperature can resolve the remaining close pair. The other pairs already meet the threshold, and the short retention time leaves ample room for increased retention.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with lower temperature to counter early-peak compression and probe a different selectivity region. This may offer a faster fully resolved alternative; injection 9 remains the fastest method with maximum CRF so far.

Test whether a modest temperature increase can preserve the critical pair at a steeper gradient and shorten retention. The early pair may become limiting, so this run will establish the useful upper-temperature boundary near the fastest fully resolved methods.

Test whether a shallower gradient can restore the middle pair's resolution at a higher starting organic fraction. Using 45 C rather than 55 C should protect early-pair selectivity while seeking another fully resolved, short-retention method.

Test a two-minute gradient with a shallower slope than injection 9 to preserve the critical separation, followed by elution of the late peaks during the hold. This explores whether a lower endpoint can shorten the programmed gradient without losing maximum CRF.

Lower injection 13's temperature by one step to restore early-pair resolution while testing whether the middle pair still meets R = 1.5. This probes a faster boundary near the best fully resolved methods; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Probe whether a higher starting organic fraction separates the middle pair on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover under a fast gradient. Low temperature should help retain the early compounds, although early-peak compression remains a risk.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower two-minute gradient to spread the close middle pair in the fast-elution region. Keeping 25 C protects early retention; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Make injection 18's gradient shallower while keeping its starting fraction and temperature fixed to test whether the middle pair reaches full resolution. The lower endpoint will delay the last peak, but its current 2.20-minute retention leaves substantial room below the time-penalty threshold.

The middle pair responded only weakly to slope in injections 18–19, so shift the solvent window upward to test selectivity instead. The early pair's resolution margin may permit this shift, potentially yielding full resolution with substantially faster elution than injection 9.

Return to 0.40 starting organic to protect the early pair, and use a modest temperature increase to test middle-pair selectivity. The intermediate endpoint balances the late-peak delay in injection 19 against the steeper gradient in injection 18.

Return to the confirmed maximum-CRF region and lower injection 9's endpoint one step to improve its marginal middle-pair resolution. Unlike injection 15, this gradient should continue through late-peak elution, avoiding the long low-organic hold.
Use the six-minute grid to obtain a slope between injections 9 and 22. This should retain maximum CRF with more critical-pair margin than injection 9 and faster last-peak elution than injection 22.

Increase injection 23's endpoint one step to test the steepest nearby gradient that might retain full resolution. This slope lies between the fully resolved injection 9 and the under-resolved injection 8, targeting a slightly faster maximum-CRF method.

Use injection 9's fully resolved slope and starting composition with a higher final organic fraction for stronger post-elution washing. This should preserve its approximately 3.40-minute last peak and maximum CRF; injection 24 indicates that a steeper slope sacrifices full resolution.
